scribe.question: A three-page report repeats its section title at the top of every page. It is a real heading, not a running header. What does scribe do with it?

options.text: Keeps it as a heading, because it is numbered like the others
Drops it, because it repeats near the edge of most pages and that is all scribe can see
Keeps the first one and drops the repeats
Keeps it, and marks the repeats for review

scribe.question: A word is split across a line break as `well-` then `being`. What comes out?

options.text: `wellbeing`, because a hyphen at a line end is the typesetter's, not the writer's
`well-being`, because a short list of prefixes is allowed to keep its hyphen
`well- being`, because the break is preserved along with the hyphen
`well-being`, because a dictionary is consulted for the compound

scribe.question: Page furniture is removed before anything looks for headings. What does that ordering cost?

options.text: Nothing: the two rules never look at the same lines
Page numbers can no longer be used to order the sections
A real heading that repeats on most pages is gone before the heading rule can see it
A heading on the first page is missed, because there is nothing before it to compare against

scribe.question: Footnote markers used to be found after any full stop, and the rule was tightened. What was going wrong?

options.text: A marker at the very end of a paragraph was being missed
Two markers next to each other were being read as one
Every decimal number in the document was being read as a footnote reference
A page number at the foot of a page was being taken for a marker

scribe.question: You want the running header kept on a one-page letter but still dropped from a long report. What stands in the way?

options.text: Markdown has no way to mark a line as a page header
Repetition across pages is the only signal there is, and one page cannot show it
The header is removed before anything could tell the two documents apart
The page number would have to be kept along with it

tally.question: You really did buy the same £3 coffee twice on the same day at the same shop. What does the summary show?

options.text: Both, because they are two separate purchases
One, because nothing in the row tells a real repeat from a repeated row
Both, with the second marked as a possible duplicate
It stops and asks which one to keep

tally.question: A row whose description mentions a transfer is left out of duplicate removal. Why?

options.text: Because a transfer is not spending, so it never reaches the totals anyway
Because the two legs of a move between your own accounts look exactly like a duplicate
Because the two legs arrive on different dates and would never collide
Because the bank marks transfers already, so the rule is not needed

tally.question: A bank export lists every amount as a positive number, spending included. What does tally do?

options.text: Refuses the file, because the direction cannot be known from it
Leaves the amounts alone and reads the direction from a separate column
Takes the file's own shape as the convention and flips every sign
Treats the largest amounts as spending and the rest as money coming in

tally.question: Amounts are rounded once at the summary rather than on every transaction. What does that give up?

options.text: Speed, because every exact amount has to be carried until the end
Agreeing line by line with a printed receipt
Being able to show the totals in another currency
Accuracy, because many small amounts drift further apart this way

tally.question: You add a rule for one coffee shop, but a broader "cafe" rule already matches it. What decides which one applies?

options.text: The more specific pattern wins, whichever order they are in
Where it sits in the list, because the first pattern that matches wins
Both apply, and the amount is split between them
Neither: two matching rules send it to the uncategorised bucket
